title: First keep yourself in peace (II.3)
hook: a peaceable person does more good than a learned one
tomorrow: what two small things lift a person off the ground?

segments.voice: Yesterday, book two opened its inner door: the kingdom of God is within you, and Christ visits the inward person like a guest. The line was within you.

The group project call is going sideways. Two people are talking over each other. The smartest one on the call has the best argument and is winning it, loudly, and everything gets worse. Then someone who hasn't said much unmutes. Slow, steady: okay, can we back up a second? The whole call exhales. The Imitation would bet on that voice. A peaceable person, chapter three of book two says, does more good than a very learned one. But before it lets anyone fix the room, it gives an order of operations.
screen: `THE CALL GOES SIDEWAYS.` → `SOMEONE UNMUTES, SLOW AND STEADY.` → `MORE GOOD THAN A LEARNED ONE.`

segments.voice: First, the order. Keep yourself in peace first, the chapter says, and then you'll be able to bring peace to others. The Latin calls that person homo pacificus, the peaceable one. Second, two people side by side. The peaceable person turns everything toward good. The heated, troubled person turns even good into evil, believes evil easily, suspects everyone, and is neither quiet himself nor lets anyone else be. Third, the mirror. The heated person keeps careful track of what others owe and forgets what he owes himself. So the Imitation says: be zealous about yourself first, and then you can fairly be zealous about your neighbor. We're quick to excuse our own deeds, it notes, and slow to accept anyone else's excuse. Fairer to accuse yourself and excuse your brother. An uncomfortable trade, and a fair one: the same patience you'd ask for, handed out first. Here's one to tell a friend tonight. The chapter says getting along with good, gentle people is no great thing; everyone likes that. Living at peace with hard, difficult people is a great grace. So the peace it means isn't a calm that needs a calm room. It starts inside, and then it walks into the loud one. That's why the brilliant argument can wait thirty seconds while the arguer breathes.
screen: `PEACE FIRST, THEN FOR OTHERS.` · `ONE TURNS ALL TO GOOD.` · `ACCUSE YOURSELF, EXCUSE YOUR BROTHER.` · `PEACE WITH THE HARD ONES.` · then, large: `A PEACEABLE PERSON DOES MORE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit up and let your shoulders drop, your jaw loosen, your hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind one person who will need something from you soon, and stay in that posture until you can picture them without bracing. No rush. If you pray, ask for peace in you first, and then in them.
First keep yourself in peace. The Imitation's order: settle your own heart, and then you can bring peace to someone else.
screen: `FIRST KEEP YOURSELF IN PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this: peace first, even when the loudest argument in the room happens to be yours. Talk tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1478 COUNTS.` → `THE IMITATION, READ THROUGH · 17 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT TWO SMALL THINGS LIFT A PERSON OFF THE GROUND?`

howItsDone: Catholics who read the Imitation often take one chapter slowly, and many bring its counsels into the examination of conscience, asking where they judged others quickly or excused themselves.

chat.says: won 2-0 but two girls almost fought in the locker room. i yelled louder than both of them. now what
options: Get calm yourself first, then talk to each one alone. Peace in you before peace for them.
Set a strict rule and enforce it. A sharp captain ends fights faster than a calm one.
Stay out of it. Peace first means guarding your own calm and letting them sort it out.

notes: Imitation II.3 paraphrased throughout: keep yourself first in peace, then you can pacify others; a peaceable man profits more than a very learned one; the passionate man turns good to evil and easily believes evil; he is neither quiet himself nor lets others be; zeal first over yourself, then over your neighbor; we excuse ourselves and won't take others' excuses; it is no great thing to live with the good and gentle, but to live peaceably with the hard and perverse is a great grace. Confirm each against the Latin.
Latin 'homo pacificus' quoted as a two-word phrase; confirm it appears in II.3 in that form. The Matthew 5:9 echo is offered only as what 'some readers hear' (trapdoor).
